title: The Blue Notebook
subject: English
source: Written for english/y7 lesson 49 (First-person account 'The Blue Notebook' (teacher-written composite drawn from experiences reported by refugee charities; not one real person's story; pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 49. A teacher-written composite account, drawn from experiences reported by refugee charities: not one real person's story. Read it, then answer the questions.

passage.title: The Blue Notebook
paras: Before we left, our street was the whole world. I knew every crack in the pavement and every cat on every wall. I drew them all in the blue notebook my teacher gave me for winning a spelling competition.

My mother gave me ten minutes. I took my school bag, my brother's hand and a blue notebook with my best drawings of our street. We walked for two nights. At the border a woman in a white jacket gave us bread and asked our names; she wrote them down slowly, as if they mattered. Now, in a new city, I am learning words for things I already know: bread, window, home. The notebook is nearly full. On the first page is our old street. On the last page I have started this one.

Some days the new words are easy. Some days my tongue is too tired for them. My brother learns faster than me; he already laughs at jokes I do not understand. But when I open the notebook and see the two streets, the old and the new, I know that I am the same person on both pages.

questions.q: Retrieve three things the writer took when leaving
questions.a: a school bag, a brother's hand and a blue notebook of drawings

questions.q: What does the notebook symbolise at the end?
questions.a: a life continuing: the old street on the first page and the new one on the last, so the writer has not lost hope

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a PEEDL paragraph: 'Compare how the poem and the account present the refugee experience.' Starter: 'Both texts show that..., however...'
questions.a: A PEEDL paragraph: both show loss and humanity; the poem speaks for all through a refrain, the account through one child's details.

questions.q: Extend: find the line that shows resilience and explain it
questions.a: 'On the last page I have started this one': the writer begins again in a new place.

questions.q: Stretch: why might a charity choose a first-person account rather than statistics?
questions.a: Personal details create empathy faster than numbers, so readers are more likely to help.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention the woman writing names down 'slowly, as if they mattered'?
options: to show being treated with dignity mattered deeply
to show the woman was slow at writing
questions.a: A) to show being treated with dignity mattered deeply. After losing everything, being treated as a person, with a name, gave the writer dignity.

questions.q: The woman at the border wrote names...
questions.a: C) slowly, as if they mattered

questions.q: Answer the ponder: what does an account do that a poem may not?
questions.a: For example: it gives one person's concrete details, so we picture a real life.
